title: St David's Day
when_text: 1 March, the day David is said to have died
intro: Dewi Sant, a 6th-century monk and bishop, became the patron saint of Wales, and his feast on 1 March has been kept since he was made a saint in about 1120. His shrine at St Davids drew pilgrims from across the Christian West, and the places of his birth, youth and best-known miracle are still marked by chapels and churches. Today the Welsh wear leeks or daffodils, eat cawl and Welsh cakes, and march in parades.

facts.title: A saint's death day
facts.text: 1 March is kept as the day David died; the year is traditionally given as 589, though the Welsh annals and later historians give other dates. His feast has been kept regularly since he was canonised by Pope Callixtus II in about 1120.

sources.title: Saint David's Day (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: falls on 1 March, the date of Saint David's death in 589 AD

sources.title: Saint David's Day (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: David was canonised in the Catholic church by Pope Callixtus II in 1120

sources.title: Saint David (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The Welsh annals placed his death 569 years after the birth of Christ, but Phillimore's dating revised this to 601.

facts.title: Born on the clifftop
facts.text: Tradition says David was born to St Non around AD 500 on the clifftop where the ruined Chapel of St Non now stands, near St Davids. The ruin is unusual in lying north to south.

sources.title: St Davids (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: David is said to have been born to Saint Non around 500 AD, at the place where the Chapel of St Non now stands.

sources.title: Chapel of St Non (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: is unusual in that it is aligned north–south rather than the usual east–west

facts.title: The ground that rose
facts.text: David's best-known miracle came at the Synod of Brefi in the 6th century: preaching to a great crowd, he stood on ground that is said to have risen into a small hill so all could hear him. The church of Llanddewi Brefi stands on that hill.

sources.title: Saint David (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: the village of Llanddewi Brefi stands on the spot where the ground on which he stood is reputed to have risen up to form a small hill

sources.title: Llanddewi Brefi (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: This event is said to have taken place on the small hill where St.

facts.title: "Do the little things"
facts.text: David's last sermon, as his medieval Life records it, urged his followers to be joyful, keep the faith and do the little things they had seen him do. "Gwnewch y pethau bychain" is still a well-known saying in Welsh.

sources.title: Saint David (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: "Do ye the little things in life" ("Gwnewch y pethau bychain mewn bywyd") is today a very well known phrase in Welsh.

facts.title: Monks who pulled their own ploughs
facts.text: David's monastic rule was famously hard: his monks pulled the plough themselves with no oxen and lived on bread, salt, herbs and water, which earned them the name "watermen".

sources.title: Saint David (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The Monastic Rule of David prescribed that monks had to pull the plough themselves without draught animals, and must eat only bread with salt and herbs and drink only water getting them the name "watermen".

facts.title: Two to St Davids, one to Rome
facts.text: In 1123 Pope Calixtus II granted St Davids a papal privilege, and it became a pilgrim centre for the whole Western church: two pilgrimages there counted as one to Rome, and three as one to Jerusalem.

sources.title: St Davids Cathedral (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: the Pope decreed that "Two pilgrimages to St Davids is equal to one to Rome, and three pilgrimages to one to Jerusalem"

facts.title: A shrine built, stripped and restored
facts.text: A new shrine for David's relics was built in 1275 and Edward I prayed at it in 1284. At the Reformation Bishop Barlow stripped its jewels and took away the relics; the restored shrine was rededicated on St David's Day 2012.

sources.title: Saint David (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: It was at this shrine that Edward I came to pray in 1284.

sources.title: Saint David (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: stripped the shrine of its jewels and confiscated the relics of David and Justinian

sources.title: Saint David (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The restored Shrine of Saint David was unveiled and rededicated by the Right Reverend Wyn Evans, Bishop of St David's, at a Choral Eucharist on Saint David's Day, 2012.

facts.title: A cathedral on a slope
facts.text: The floor of St Davids Cathedral, begun in 1181, falls nearly four metres from east to west, and the building is still moving very slightly.

sources.title: St Davids Cathedral (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: There is a pronounced slope to the floor of the cathedral, amounting to a height difference of nearly four metres between the east and west ends, and the building is still shifting minutely.

facts.title: Why the leek?
facts.text: The leek, or the daffodil (in Welsh "Peter's leek"), is worn on the day. One Welsh story says King Cadwaladr had his men wear leeks in a battle against the Saxons fought in a leek field; the Elizabethan poet Michael Drayton said instead that David ate only leeks when fasting.

sources.title: Leek (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: King Cadwaladr of Gwynedd ordered his soldiers to identify themselves by wearing the vegetable on their helmets in an ancient battle against the Saxons that took place in a leek field

sources.title: Leek (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The Elizabethan poet Michael Drayton stated, in contrast, that the tradition was a tribute to Saint David, who ate only leeks when he was fasting.

facts.title: Shakespeare's leek
facts.text: By Shakespeare's time wearing a leek was already old: in Henry V the king tells the Welsh captain Fluellen that he wears one too, "for I am Welsh".

sources.title: Leek (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Shakespeare, for example, refers to the custom of wearing a leek as an "ancient tradition" in Henry V

sources.title: Leek (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: In the play, Henry V tells the Welsh officer Fluellen that he, too, is wearing a leek "for I am Welsh, you know, good countryman."

facts.title: A Welsh king's feast in London, and its enemies
facts.text: Henry VII, of Welsh descent, paid for St David's Day celebrations for his household and had Welsh mead and cheese brought to his court. A century and a half later Samuel Pepys saw Londoners answer the Welsh celebrations by hanging and burning life-sized effigies of Welshmen.

sources.title: Saint David's Day (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Henry regularly funded Saint David’s Day celebrations for his Palace staff, ordering Welsh mead and cheeses to be brought from Wales to his court in London

sources.title: Saint David's Day (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The 17th-century diarist Samuel Pepys noted how Saint David's Day celebrations by the Welsh in London would spark anti-Welsh counter-celebrations, including the burning and symbolic lynching of life-sized effigies of Welshmen.

facts.title: Cawl and Welsh cakes
facts.text: The dishes of the day are cawl (a soup), bara brith tea loaf, Welsh cakes, Welsh lamb and Welsh rarebit.

sources.title: Saint David's Day (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Popular dishes traditionally eaten on Saint David's Day include cawl (soup), bara brith tea loaf, Welsh Cakes, Welsh lamb and Welsh rarebit.

facts.title: Parades, but no holiday
facts.text: Towns across Wales hold parades, the largest in Cardiff. Unlike St Patrick's Day in Ireland it is not a public holiday: the National Assembly voted unanimously for one in 2000, but a petition for a bank holiday was turned down by Downing Street in 2007.

sources.title: Saint David's Day (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Around Wales each year, Saint David is commemorated in parades, the largest of which is in Cardiff.

sources.title: Saint David's Day (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.locator: section Proposals for a public holiday
sources.quote: Cross-party support resulted in the National Assembly for Wales voting unanimously to make Saint David's Day a public holiday in 2000.

sources.title: Saint David's Day (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.locator: section Proposals for a public holiday
sources.quote: A petition in 2007 to make Saint David's Day a bank holiday was rejected by the office of the British Prime Minister Tony Blair.

facts.title: Britain's smallest city
facts.text: Thanks to its cathedral St Davids is a city, the smallest in the United Kingdom by population. It lost the status in 1886 and had it restored by the Queen in 1994.

sources.title: St Davids (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: St Davids is the United Kingdom's smallest city by population

sources.title: St Davids (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: City status was lost in 1886, but restored in 1994 at the request of Queen Elizabeth II.

places.name: St Davids Cathedral
places.why: Built on the site of David's monastery in the Glyn Rhosyn valley; his shrine here was a great pilgrim goal of the Middle Ages.

sources.title: Saint David (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: St David's Cathedral stands on the site of the monastery he founded in the Glyn Rhosyn valley of Pembrokeshire.

sources.title: Saint David (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: where his shrine was a popular place of pilgrimage throughout the Middle Ages

places.name: St Davids Bishop's Palace
places.why: Ruined medieval palace of the bishops beside the cathedral, largely the work of Bishop Henry de Gower (1328-47), with its arcaded parapet; in the care of Cadw.

sources.title: St Davids Bishop's Palace (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: is a ruined medieval episcopal palace located adjacent to St Davids Cathedral

sources.title: St Davids Bishop's Palace (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The man responsible for much of the site that can be seen today was Bishop Henry de Gower (1328–1347).

places.name: Chapel of St Non
places.why: Ruined clifftop chapel held by tradition to mark David's birthplace and thought to be one of the oldest Christian buildings in Wales; a medieval pilgrim stop, now in the care of Cadw.

sources.title: Chapel of St Non (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The ruin is thought to be on the site of St Non's house and to be one of the oldest Christian buildings in Wales.

places.name: St Non's Well
places.why: Holy well beside St Non's chapel, thought to cure eye trouble; in 1717 people still left pins and pebbles here on St Non's Day, 2 March, the day after David's.

sources.title: Chapel of St Non (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: especially upon St. Nun's Day (March 2nd) which they kept holy, and offer Pins, Pebbles, Etc at this well

sources.title: Chapel of St Non (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: It was thought to be particularly effective for eye problems

places.name: St David's Church, Llanddewi Brefi
places.why: Stands on the hill said to have risen under David at the Synod of Brefi; a collegiate church founded here by Bishop Thomas Bek in 1187.

sources.title: Llanddewi Brefi (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The construction of the Norman church is credited to Thomas Bek, Bishop of St Davids, who built it as a collegiate church for the establishment which he is said to have founded here in 1187.

places.name: St David's Church, Henfynyw
places.why: Ancient church in Ceredigion where David was said to have spent some of his early years; it has an inscribed stone of AD 600-800 in its east wall.

sources.title: Henfynyw (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.locator: section Henfynyw church and St. David
sources.quote: early Christian lore had it that Henfynyw was the place where St David had spent some of his early years

sources.title: Henfynyw (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.locator: section Henfynyw church and St. David
sources.quote: Henfynyw church is ancient and has an inscribed stone in the east wall dated to the period 600–800 AD

places.name: Porthclais
places.why: Little harbour near St Davids where David is said to have been baptised by St Elvis.

sources.title: St Davids (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: He was baptised by Saint Elvis at Porthclais

places.name: Glastonbury Abbey
places.why: David's medieval biographer Rhygyfarch counted Glastonbury among his foundations; William of Malmesbury said David only rededicated it and gave it a great sapphire altar.

sources.title: Saint David (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Rhigyfarch counted Glastonbury Abbey among the churches David founded.

sources.title: Saint David (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: said that David visited Glastonbury only to rededicate the Abbey and to donate a travelling altar including a great sapphire
